title: Solid-State Batteries: Why Aren't They in Your Car Yet? 🔋🧪 #shorts

scenes.text: Solid-state batteries promise more range in the same space. So where are they?
Today's EV cells move lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte, and that liquid can burn.
Solid-state cells swap it for a thin solid layer, allowing a lithium-metal anode that holds far more charge than graphite.
The catch: solids don't flow. Electrodes swell and shrink while charging, gaps open, so cells must be kept squeezed.
And lithium can grow needles called dendrites that crack the layer and short the cell.
Still, in twenty twenty-five a Mercedes test car with lithium-metal solid-state cells drove seven hundred forty-nine miles on one charge.
Toyota aims for twenty twenty-seven or eight. Would you wait? Follow EV Drive.
